items.title: L9: How Behaviour levels rise with grade
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Each of the nine Behaviours is described at several levels, and the level rises with the grade. The wording differs between Behaviours, but the pattern is consistent. At the lowest levels, which are usually used for AA and AO roles, the focus is on your own work, your immediate team and doing things well with some guidance. At the next level, usually used for EO roles, you are expected to guide or coordinate others, take more responsibility for results and make some decisions on your own. At the levels usually used for HEO and SEO roles, the focus moves to leading a team or area, managing performance and resources, influencing people beyond your own line and making decisions that affect others. Higher grades add further scope: shaping direction across a function, managing risk and representing the organisation externally. Two features mark a step up. The first is scope, meaning how many people or how large an area your actions affect. The second is independence, meaning how far you work out what to do rather than being told. A Changing and Improving example at AO level might be a better layout for one form. At EO level it might be a new routine adopted by a small team. At HEO level it might be redesigning a process that crosses teams, with a business case and measured benefits. The same story rarely fits two grades without changes, so tailor the emphasis. Advertised roles state the level of each Behaviour, so check the wording before you choose an example, and match its scope to the level asked for.

questions.prompt: Which two features most clearly mark a step up from one grade's Behaviour level to the next?

options.text: Scope and independence
Length of service and the number of courses completed
Formal qualifications and the size of the job title
Hours worked and the number of customers served

questions.hint: Scope means how many people or how large an area is affected; independence means working out what to do.

questions.prompt: An AO-level Changing and Improving example is most likely to involve what?

options.text: A redesign of a process that crosses several teams, with a business case
A change to departmental policy agreed with senior managers
A new contract for an IT system used across the department
A better layout for a single form that she uses herself

questions.prompt: Which example best fits Changing and Improving at HEO level?

options.text: Suggesting a neater folder layout to a supervisor for the team's shared drive
Following an updated checklist faithfully for several months
Noticing a typing error in a standard letter and reporting it
Redesigning a process that crosses teams and showing measured benefits

questions.hint: HEO evidence involves wider scope and rigour.

questions.prompt: At EO level, which expectation is usually added to the AO focus on own work?

options.text: Setting the strategy for a whole department
Representing the organisation to external partners
Guiding or coordinating the work of others
Managing a large budget and signing off spending

questions.prompt: Where does an advert state the level at which each Behaviour is assessed?

options.text: In the department's staff handbook, which lists the expected levels for every grade
In the role's Success Profile information attached to the advert
On the pay scale table published for the grade
In the confirmation email received after applying

questions.prompt: A candidate uses the same story for AO and HEO applications. What is the likely problem?

options.text: The scope will be too small for HEO unless emphasis and detail are adapted
Assessors never accept a story that has been used in an earlier application
The Behaviours assessed at HEO are entirely different from those at AO
HEO applications may not use examples from voluntary or home settings

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical addition at SEO level and above?

options.text: Learning the basic procedures of the team and following them closely
Following a team leader's instructions on day-to-day casework
Shaping direction across a function and managing risk
Checking one's own work for accuracy before it is sent

questions.prompt: What does 'independence' mean as a feature of a step up?

options.text: Working alone, away from the team, on a self-chosen task
Refusing advice so that decisions are wholly your own
Working out what to do rather than waiting to be told
Choosing your own hours and place of work

questions.prompt: Which statement about the nine Behaviour names across grades is accurate?

options.text: Each grade is assessed on a different set of Behaviours with different names
Only senior grades are assessed on Behaviours; lower grades use Strengths
Behaviours replace Strengths and Ability at higher grades
The names stay the same but the level of expectation rises with grade

questions.prompt: An HEO assessor reads an answer about a task the candidate did well on her own, with no influence on others. How might it be judged?

options.text: Relevant, but pitched below the grade's level
Excellent, because quality of work matters more than scale
Irrelevant, because working alone cannot show the Behaviour
A sign of strong Leadership, since she acted without supervision

items.title: L9: What EO-level evidence looks like
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: EO roles typically sit between entry level and management. The Behaviours at this level usually ask you to guide others, take ownership of a piece of work and contribute to improvements. Good EO evidence therefore often includes a small number of people, a task with some complexity and your own decisions. Consider Communicating and Influencing at EO level. An AO answer might describe explaining a process clearly to a customer. An EO answer might describe explaining a changed process to colleagues with varied views, adapting the message for each and winning agreement. Leadership at EO level is typically shown by setting an example, supporting colleagues, keeping people informed and taking responsibility for a result, not by formal line management. Developing Self and Others at EO level often includes helping a new starter reach competence, in addition to your own learning. Managing a Quality Service at EO level may include reviewing others' work against the standard, or tracking errors and acting on patterns. Delivering at Pace at EO level may include planning a small team's work for a week, tracking progress and rebalancing. A frequent weakness is writing an EO answer that is really an AO answer with a bigger vocabulary. To check, ask: whose work did I affect besides my own, what decisions did I take without being told, and what changed for the service? If the answers are 'nobody', 'none' and 'nothing', the example is probably pitched too low. Note that EO evidence does not require a formal supervisory title.

questions.prompt: Which feature most reliably lifts an AO-style answer to EO level?

options.text: Longer sentences and more formal, senior-sounding vocabulary
Evidence of guiding others and taking decisions of your own
More detail about the customer and how the problem arose
A reference to the department's name and the team's purpose

questions.prompt: Which is the best EO-level example of Developing Self and Others?

options.text: Completing a mandatory training course on time
Helping a new starter reach competence and checking their work
Reading the intranet guidance on a new procedure
Asking a manager for feedback once a year

questions.prompt: What does the 'check' of three questions test?

options.text: Whether the answer fits within the word limit
Whether the story is true and could be verified by a referee
Whether the Behaviour name is mentioned in the answer
Whether the example is pitched at the right level for the grade

questions.hint: Whose work, which decisions, what changed.

questions.prompt: Which description fits Leadership at EO level?

options.text: Formally line-managing a large team and its whole budget for the year
Setting objectives and ratings for staff in other departments
Setting an example, supporting colleagues and owning a result
Directing departmental policy and approving spending

questions.prompt: Which activity is good EO evidence for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Checking only your own cases very carefully before sending them out
Reviewing others' work against the standard and acting on error patterns
Following the call script exactly on every call and noting any deviations
Handling one complaint calmly and apologising

questions.prompt: For EO, Delivering at Pace might include what?

options.text: Completing a single task on time without being reminded by anyone
Following a rota prepared by a manager
Planning a small team's week and rebalancing the work
Working extra hours when a deadline is close

questions.prompt: Does EO-level evidence need a formal supervisory title?

options.text: It does not; guiding others can be shown without a title
It does, because EO is defined as a supervisory grade
It does, but only for the Leadership Behaviour
It does for every Behaviour assessed at EO level

questions.prompt: An EO answer says: 'I explained the changed process to my colleagues.' What would raise it?

options.text: How she adapted the message for different views and won agreement
A fuller step-by-step description of the changed process
The names and job titles of the colleagues she briefed
The date and time of the briefing

questions.prompt: What is a frequent weakness in EO answers?

options.text: An answer that is too short to be read in a minute by the assessor
An AO-level answer written with a bigger vocabulary
A missing job title at the start of the answer
Too many numbers in the Result

questions.prompt: If the answers to 'whose work did I affect besides mine' are 'nobody', what follows?

options.text: The example is probably pitched too low for EO
The answer should be rewritten and submitted for an AO role
The story must be untrue or exaggerated
The Behaviour is Leadership, not the one being asked about

items.title: L9: What HEO-level evidence looks like
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: At HEO level the Behaviours usually require you to lead a team or a defined area of work, set direction, manage performance and resources, and influence people beyond your own line. A HEO answer is therefore expected to show responsibility for outcomes that depend on other people, decisions made in the face of competing demands and an awareness of wider consequences. Take Making Effective Decisions. An EO answer may describe weighing two options for her own team. A HEO answer would more likely describe a decision with unclear information, where she consulted stakeholders, assessed risks, took a decision, explained it and accepted accountability, including when some people disagreed. Take Working Together. HEO evidence often shows building relationships with other teams or external partners and resolving conflict between competing interests. Take Developing Self and Others: HEO evidence typically includes setting objectives, giving regular and honest feedback, handling a performance concern fairly and developing someone's career. Leadership at HEO level includes setting a clear direction, motivating the team through change and challenging poor practice. Note that line management itself is not the evidence; what matters is how you led. If you do not manage staff, consider examples where you led a project, chaired a group, coordinated across teams or led a piece of work through influence. Be careful with confidential or personal details of staff; describe a performance concern in general terms, such as 'a team member who was missing deadlines', and focus on what you did, not on private circumstances.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes a HEO Making Effective Decisions answer from an EO one?

options.text: Decisions made with unclear information, consulting stakeholders and owning the outcome
Choosing between two options for her own team using clear figures and recording it
Following the policy accurately and recording the outcome
Checking figures twice before sending a report

questions.prompt: Which activity is typical HEO-level Developing Self and Others evidence?

options.text: Attending a course and writing up in detail what she has learned from it
Completing a personal development plan for the year and discussing it
Shadowing a more experienced colleague for a week to see how she works
Setting objectives, giving honest feedback and handling a performance concern fairly

questions.prompt: Does line management itself count as evidence at HEO level?

options.text: It does not; the evidence is how you led, not the title
It does, because holding a management post proves leadership
It does, but only if the team has more than ten people
It does, if the team sits together in one office

questions.prompt: A candidate who manages no staff applies for a HEO role. Which example could she use for Leadership?

options.text: Describing only her own duties in the current post in more detail
Leading a project or coordinating teams through influence
Describing the work her manager carries out
Describing the history and structure of her team

questions.prompt: How should a performance concern in the team be described in an application?

options.text: With the person's name and job title so the panel can check
In general terms, focusing on what you did, not private circumstances
With the medical details that explained the performance problem
As a complaint about the person's attitude and conduct

questions.prompt: Which Working Together example is typical at HEO level?

options.text: Helping a colleague who sits nearby to find a form she is looking for
Resolving conflict between the competing interests of two teams
Joining the weekly team meeting and taking notes
Sharing a rota that a manager has written

questions.prompt: Which element of a decision story shows accountability?

options.text: Delaying the decision until every fact was clear
Passing the decision to a manager to avoid criticism
Asking everyone to vote so the choice was shared
Explaining the decision and accepting responsibility when some disagreed

questions.prompt: At HEO level, Leadership includes which of these?

options.text: Following instructions closely and reporting progress to the manager each week
Doing much of the team's work personally
Checking attendance and approving leave
Setting a clear direction and challenging poor practice

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the scope of HEO evidence?

options.text: Tasks done entirely alone and checked by a supervisor
Outcomes that depend on other people and have wider consequences
Tasks set by a supervisor with a clear method
Routine casework with a fixed procedure

questions.prompt: Why is 'I managed a team of five' alone weak HEO evidence?

options.text: It is too short to fill a Behaviour answer and gives the assessor no detail
It names a title without showing how she led
It is too long for the word limit
It refers to people and not to results

questions.hint: The title does not show behaviour.

items.title: L9: SEO expectations and leading beyond your team
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: SEO roles usually manage a larger team or several teams, or lead a specialist or policy area, and they work with senior stakeholders. The Behaviours at this level generally require evidence of shaping direction, managing through others (including managers), balancing competing priorities across an area and representing the organisation to others. The step up from HEO is mainly about breadth, complexity and the use of influence without relying on formal authority. For Seeing the Big Picture, SEO evidence might show how you aligned your area's plan to departmental priorities, anticipated external changes and adjusted resources. For Managing a Quality Service, it might show setting standards, using data to find service problems and holding teams to account. For Delivering at Pace, it would show planning across teams, managing risks to delivery and making trade-offs openly. For Working Together, it often involves building coalitions among groups with competing aims. For Communicating and Influencing, it includes briefing senior people concisely, negotiating and managing difficult messages. For Changing and Improving, it includes leading change that people resist, with a sound case and a plan for adoption. Evidence should show you leading others to lead, which means developing and supporting managers beneath you. A typical SEO weakness is describing personal heroics: staying late and doing the work yourself. Panels at this level want to see how you built capability and sustained results without depending on you alone. Also expect probing on how you handled things that went wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the main step up from HEO to SEO evidence?

options.text: Breadth, complexity and influence without relying on formal authority
More hours of work and a heavier caseload
More qualifications and professional memberships
A more formal and technical writing style

questions.prompt: Which is a typical SEO weakness?

options.text: Personal heroics, such as staying late to do the work herself
Describing how she delegated work to her managers over the year
Describing a development plan for a team leader
Describing a risk register that she maintained

questions.prompt: What does 'leading others to lead' mean?

options.text: Taking over their decisions when they hesitate
Developing and supporting the managers beneath you
Leading from the front on every task personally
Removing layers of management to speed up decisions

questions.prompt: Which example best shows SEO-level Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: Understanding how her own task affects the rest of the team
Aligning her area's plan to departmental priorities and adjusting resources for external change
Following the instructions in a department-wide memo
Reading the department's annual report each year

questions.prompt: Which example best shows SEO-level Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Checking her own cases carefully before they are sent
Answering complaints politely and accurately
Setting standards, using data to find problems and holding teams to account
Following a checklist for each case

questions.prompt: For Delivering at Pace at SEO level, what should be shown?

options.text: Completing her own work on time, every time, without reminders
Asking for extra time whenever a deadline looks close
Planning across teams, managing delivery risks and making trade-offs openly
Reporting progress to her manager every week

questions.prompt: What does building a coalition involve in Working Together at SEO level?

options.text: Bringing groups with competing aims behind a shared approach
Making a single team agree to her plan after a long discussion
Avoiding disagreement by leaving contentious points out
Sending a group email asking everyone to cooperate

questions.prompt: What do panels want to see in SEO evidence of results?

options.text: How capability was built so results lasted without her
How many hours were worked in total to reach the result
How quickly instructions were given to the team members
How few complaints staff made about the workload

questions.prompt: What kind of follow-up question should an SEO candidate expect?

options.text: What would you do with an extra month's holiday?
Which of the nine Behaviours is your favourite?
How did you handle things that went wrong?
How many cases did you process last week?

questions.prompt: For Communicating and Influencing at SEO level, which activity is typical?

options.text: Writing a clear reply to a customer's letter and checking the facts first
Explaining a form to an applicant
Answering telephone enquiries in a polite manner
Briefing senior people concisely and managing difficult messages

items.title: L9: Spotting an under-pitched answer
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: An under-pitched answer is one that may be well written and honest, yet describes evidence below the level of the grade being recruited for. The assessor cannot score what the candidate could have done, only what the answer shows. Typical signs are a task with no impact on anyone else, a decision taken with a clear rule to follow, no sign of independence, and a result confined to one person or one case. Consider a HEO Delivering at Pace answer: 'I had 30 forms to process by Friday. I sorted them by date and completed them by Thursday.' The planning is sound but the scope is one person's workload with a ready-made deadline. To lift it, the candidate might choose a different example: leading a team of six through a spike in demand, negotiating with another team to borrow staff, escalating a risk to her manager with options, and communicating the changes to customers. A common reaction is to add adjectives to the same facts. This does not help. A better method is to ask what was the largest piece of work you were responsible for, who else depended on you and what judgement you used. If the answer is that you do not have a bigger example, look at voluntary or other settings or consider stretch tasks you could take on and apply later. Remember that an assessor does not know you have more to offer; they can only read the page. Another sign is a lack of reasons. If the answer says what was done but not why, it is also under-pitched, because senior roles are expected to make and explain judgements.

questions.prompt: The HEO pace answer says 'I had 30 forms to process by Friday and completed them by Thursday.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: The deadline given was too tight to be realistic
The number of forms was too large for one person
The Result is not given as a number
The scope is one person's workload with a ready-made deadline

questions.prompt: Which change would lift that answer most?

options.text: Adding stronger adjectives to describe the same facts
Choosing a bigger example, such as leading a team through a demand spike
Making the sentences longer and more formal
Naming the type of form and the department

questions.prompt: Why does adding adjectives to the same facts rarely help?

options.text: The scope and judgement shown remain the same
Assessors penalise adjectives in written evidence
They use up words that are needed for the Result
They make the story seem untrue to a panel

questions.prompt: Which question helps find a better example?

options.text: What is the quickest piece of work I have ever finished for anyone?
What did my manager do in the same situation as mine?
What was the largest piece of work I was responsible for?
What task did I enjoy most in my current job?

questions.prompt: What can a candidate do if she has no bigger example?

options.text: Exaggerate the existing example so that it appears larger
Look at voluntary settings, or take on stretch tasks to use later
Leave the Behaviour out and hope the panel does not notice
Use an example from a colleague's work instead

questions.prompt: Which sign shows an answer is under-pitched for senior roles?

options.text: It contains a number in the Result
It says what was done but gives no reason why
It uses the word 'I' for the candidate's actions
It has a Result at the end

questions.prompt: What can an assessor score?

options.text: What the candidate could have done with more words
What the candidate's referee is likely to say
Only what the answer shows
What the candidate's manager thinks of her

questions.prompt: Which feature suggests a lack of independence?

options.text: A decision made after consulting stakeholders and weighing the risks of each option
A clear rule to follow, with no judgement needed
A plan she designed and tested herself
A risk she spotted and raised unprompted

questions.prompt: In the lifted example, which action shows influence beyond her own line?

options.text: Sorting the forms by date received and working through them in order
Negotiating with another team to borrow staff
Working late to finish before the deadline
Completing the forms accurately

questions.prompt: Which result is more convincing for the lifted example?

options.text: The forms were completed accurately by the deadline that had been set
She felt satisfied with her effort and the way the week went
Demand was met on time across the team, with customers informed
The manager seemed content with the outcome and said so to her

items.title: L9: Spotting overclaiming and misleading answers
items.body: Panels read many answers and become alert to claims that do not hold up. Overclaiming happens when the candidate presents a team's work as personal work, inflates numbers, or states a result that the actions could not have produced. Misleading answers may be unintentional. A candidate may say 'I led a project that saved the council £50,000' when she contributed to part of it. Warning signs include sweeping outcomes with very thin actions, 'we' in the Action with 'I' in the Result, precise figures with no source, and descriptions of strategic decisions by someone whose role makes this unlikely. Panels respond by asking probing questions: What exactly did you do? Who else was involved? How was the saving calculated? What would have happened if you had not acted? Honest candidates can answer these calmly. The Civil Service Code requires honesty, and false information in an application may be treated as a disciplinary matter or lead to withdrawal of an offer. To avoid overclaiming, use 'I' for your own actions and 'we' for the group's, give your contribution as a share if necessary ('I wrote the business case; the finance team calculated the saving'), describe sources of figures, and avoid causal claims you cannot support. For example, 'complaints fell after I introduced the new letter' is stronger when followed by 'although staffing also rose that month'. A candid statement of limits is a sign of integrity, and panels rate it positively. Also be wary of buzzwords that signal little real content, such as 'stakeholder engagement' without a description of who, how and what happened.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is a warning sign of overclaiming?

options.text: 'We' in the Action but 'I' in the Result
'I' in both the Action and the Result
A modest Result with a named source
A clear description of own tasks in the Action

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I led a project that saved £50,000' but only wrote part of the business case. What is the best correction?

options.text: 'I saved the council £50,000 through a project I led.'
'The project I was part of saved £50,000 in total.'
'I wrote the business case; finance calculated the saving.'
'We saved some money on the contract.'

questions.prompt: Which question will a panel use to test a precise figure?

options.text: What did you wear to the first meeting?
Where did you park on the first day?
How was the saving calculated?
Who was the most senior person you met?

questions.prompt: Why is 'complaints fell after I introduced the new letter, although staffing also rose that month' strong?

options.text: It contradicts itself, so the claim cannot be believed
It acknowledges other factors honestly
It shortens the answer to fit the limit
It avoids using any numbers

questions.prompt: What may happen if false information is found in an application?

options.text: Nothing, provided the interview goes well
It can lead to disciplinary action or an offer being withdrawn
A letter of advice is sent and the application continues
The applicant is given another chance to correct it

questions.prompt: Which phrase is a buzzword with little content?

options.text: 'I met the three tenant groups each month to agree the repairs list.'
'I wrote to the supplier asking for the delivery date.'
'I led stakeholder engagement.'
'I calculated the cost per case from the logged times.'

questions.prompt: Why do panels ask 'What would have happened if you had not acted?'

options.text: To embarrass the candidate in front of other applicants
To test whether the result can be attributed to the candidate
To fill the time left in the interview
To check how well the candidate remembers dates

questions.prompt: Which action avoids a causal claim you cannot support?

options.text: Claiming the whole of the improvement as your own
Leaving out the figures so no claim can be challenged
Describing what changed and noting other contributing factors
Blaming the previous process for the problems

questions.prompt: How should 'we' and 'I' be used to avoid overclaiming?

options.text: 'I' for your own actions and 'we' for the group's
'We' for everything, to sound modest and to share the credit with the team
'I' for everything, to show ownership
Neither word, using the passive voice throughout

questions.prompt: Which statement about a candid statement of limits is correct?

options.text: It lowers the score, because it admits weakness
It is unnecessary, since panels assume that candidates have given their best
Panels rate it positively as a sign of integrity
It is forbidden in written applications

items.title: L9: Results that mislead
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Not every misleading answer contains a false statement. Some give a true figure that creates a wrong impression, which assessors at senior levels are trained to spot. Four patterns are common. First, a missing baseline: 'we processed 500 cases in a month' means little without knowing the normal number. Second, a selected measure: reporting speed gains and omitting a rise in errors. Third, confusion of correlation and cause: 'complaints fell after my change' when complaints always fall in that season. Fourth, percentages on small numbers: 'errors fell by 50 per cent' when they went from two to one. Honest reporting gives the baseline, the measure, the period and the context. A balanced version might read: 'Between April and June, average handling time fell from 14 to 11 minutes, and quality checks showed the error rate unchanged at about 3 per cent. The same period last year saw no fall.' Notice the use of a comparison and the check on a second measure. Calculations must be right: a fall from 14 to 11 minutes is 3 minutes, which is 3 divided by 14, about 21 per cent. A fall from 40 to 30 per cent is ten percentage points, not ten per cent; confusing percentage points with percentages is a classic error that panels notice. Candidates should be ready to show how any figure was produced. If you do not have a full dataset, say what you observed and be clear about the limits of what it shows.

questions.prompt: Handling time fell from 14 to 11 minutes. What is the percentage fall, to the nearest whole number?

options.text: 3 per cent
21 per cent
27 per cent
79 per cent

questions.prompt: A rate falls from 40 per cent to 30 per cent. How should the change be described?

options.text: A fall of ten percentage points
A fall of ten per cent
A fall of thirty per cent
A fall of forty per cent

questions.prompt: Which error is made by 'errors fell by 50 per cent' when they went from two to one?

options.text: Using the wrong baseline for the comparison between the two periods
Leaving out the period over which the change occurred
Confusing percentage points with percentages
Using a percentage on a very small number, which exaggerates change

questions.prompt: Why does 'we processed 500 cases in a month' mislead on its own?

options.text: 500 is too large a number to be credible
A month is too long a period for a fair measure
It uses the word 'we' and so hides the candidate's part
There is no baseline to show whether 500 is high or low

questions.prompt: What is a 'selected measure'?

options.text: Choosing a month at random to report instead of the whole period
Using a sample of cases instead of all cases
Reporting speed gains while leaving out a rise in errors
Showing the results on a graph instead of a table

questions.prompt: Which sentence confuses correlation with cause?

options.text: 'Handling time fell from 14 to 11 minutes between April and June'
'The error rate stayed at about 3 per cent throughout'
'The same period last year saw no fall at all'
'Complaints fell after my change', when they always fall in that season

questions.prompt: What does honest reporting give?

options.text: Only the best figure, to make the point clearly
The baseline, the measure, the period and the context
Only the percentage change, with no starting figure
Only the cause, with the figures and the period left out of the answer

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to report error rate alongside handling time?

options.text: It shortens the answer so that it fits the word limit
It makes the answer harder for a panel to follow
It replaces the need for a baseline figure
It shows the faster process did not reduce quality

questions.prompt: A candidate lacks a full dataset. What should she do?

options.text: Invent plausible figures to make the Result stronger
Leave the Result out of the answer altogether
Say what she observed and be clear about its limits
Ask the panel to supply the data for her

questions.prompt: From 20 per cent to 25 per cent is a rise of how much?

options.text: Five per cent
Five percentage points
Twenty-five per cent
Ten per cent

items.title: L9: Using your current role to evidence a promotion
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles, Civil Service Commission
items.body: Promotion applications in the Civil Service are assessed on the Success Profiles for the higher grade, and under the Recruitment Principles, appointments are made on merit following fair and open competition. Internal candidates therefore compete on the same evidence standards as external ones. The best preparation starts months before an advert appears: look at the Success Profiles for the next grade, identify the gaps between your current evidence and what is expected, and seek out work that fills them. This may include acting up temporarily, leading a small project, covering a manager's duties for a period, mentoring a new starter, deputising at meetings or taking responsibility for a process. Keep a record of such evidence soon after it happens, noting the situation, your actions and the result, ideally with a figure or a comment from someone else. Then choose examples carefully: use your current role, but emphasise the parts where you operated at or beyond your grade. A well-chosen example may be a time you led others without being their manager. Do not assume that assessors know your work. An internal panel member may know you, but they still score the written evidence and may be told to disregard personal knowledge. Do not rely on your good reputation or on years in post. Length of service is not evidence of the Behaviours. Ask for feedback from colleagues and your manager on where your evidence is strong, and consider a development conversation to plan the gaps. A candidate who has built stretch evidence over a year is generally better placed than one who tries to create it the week before applying.

questions.prompt: On what basis are Civil Service appointments made, under the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Seniority within the existing grade
Merit, following fair and open competition
Length of service in the department
A recommendation from the candidate's own manager

questions.prompt: Which preparation is most valuable for an internal promotion?

options.text: Wait until an advert appears before thinking about it

items.title: L9: Choosing and distributing examples across an application
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: When an application asks for evidence of several Behaviours, a common mistake is to use the same story for more than one, or to choose stories one at a time without considering the whole set. A better approach is to treat your examples as a portfolio. First, list the Behaviours asked for. Second, brainstorm candidate stories, noting for each the Behaviours it supports and its level. Third, allocate: give each Behaviour the story where it is the main thing you did, and avoid using the same story twice unless the advert allows it. Fourth, spread your examples across different periods and settings where possible, so that the application shows range and consistency rather than a single moment. If you can show a recent example, this is often better than one from years ago, though an older but stronger example can still be used. Fifth, check that at least one example shows the scale expected at the grade. Sixth, prepare backups, because panels may ask for a different example at interview. Where the same strong story fits two Behaviours, use it once for the Behaviour where it scores highest and find another for the second. If you genuinely only have one story, vary the emphasis and say clearly which part is separate. Keep a copy of what you submit, because you will need to recall the details at interview. Tailor the vocabulary to the advert without copying its wording into your answer, since assessors want evidence of what you did, not echoes of the Behaviour description.

items.title: L9: Strengths and probing at HEO interviews
items.body: At HEO and above, interview panels often combine Behaviour questions, strengths questions and probing follow-ups. The panel will go deeper than at AO or EO level, because the role requires judgement under uncertainty. Expect questions such as: What did you consider before deciding? What risks did you identify and how did you manage them? Who disagreed and what did you do? What would you do differently now? What did you learn about your own leadership? A common pattern is the layered probe. After you finish a STAR answer, the panel asks about one element in detail, then another. A candidate whose story is real handles this calmly; a candidate who has memorised the written version without remembering the details may falter. Strengths questions at this level may ask about how you handle ambiguity, how you influence people who do not report to you, or what energises you in a leadership role. Honest answers can mention areas where you are still developing, if you describe what you do about them. A reflective answer is generally valued more than a flawless one. Time management matters: aim for answers of around two to three minutes, enough to cover the situation, your actions and the result without rambling. If you realise midway that your answer has drifted, it is acceptable to say so and return to the point. Ask for clarification if a question is ambiguous. Silence of a few seconds to think is acceptable. At the close, avoid adding new claims that you cannot support.

items.title: L9: Evidencing mistakes and what went wrong
items.body: Senior panels often ask about mistakes and failures. They are not looking for perfection; they want to see ownership, learning and how you responded to protect the service. A strong account of a mistake follows a clear pattern. Describe what went wrong without excuses or blame. State your part honestly. Describe what you did immediately to limit the harm, such as telling the right people and putting things right. Explain what you learned and what you changed so that it does not recur. For example: 'I sent a briefing with an out-of-date figure to a senior colleague. I noticed within the hour, phoned her before she used it, sent the correct figure with a note, and told my manager. I now check figures against the source and put the date of the data in the first line.' This shows honesty, speed, remediation and prevention. Weak accounts blame others ('the data was wrong') or minimise ('it was only a small error'), or describe a mistake so trivial that it shows no learning. Equally weak is an account of a disaster with no learning. Be careful about confidential details: describe the type of error without naming individuals or revealing protected information. In a Behaviour answer, a mistake can be an element of the story rather than the whole, for example an initial plan that failed and the way you adapted. At interview, a mistake that you describe calmly will not count against you, and openness about errors reflects the honesty and integrity valued in the Civil Service Code.

items.title: L9: Reviewing a whole application for level and balance
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Before submitting an application at EO, HEO or SEO level, it is worth reviewing it as an assessor would, with a checklist. First, level: does each example show the scope and independence expected at the grade? Second, match: does each answer show the Behaviour asked for, with the main Action matching that Behaviour? Third, evidence: is there a clear role for you, with 'I' for your own actions and specific verbs? Fourth, Result: does each answer give an outcome and some form of evidence, and is any figure accurate and calculable? Fifth, balance: are the examples distributed across Behaviours and settings, and have you avoided repeating the same story? Sixth, honesty: could you defend every claim at interview, including numbers and your share of the work? Seventh, clarity: is the answer short enough to be read in a minute, with the key action easy to find? Eighth, limits: does the answer stay within the word count, and does the system accept all of it? Finally, read it aloud or ask someone to read it, since errors in spelling and grammar can distract and suggest carelessness, particularly in roles where accuracy matters. You might also ask a colleague to review an example for level: would they recognise it as HEO-standard? If they think it reads as EO, consider strengthening scope or choosing a different example. Keep a note of feedback for future applications. Treat each application as practice, because the evidence you gather for one often serves the next.
